questions.q: What role does shared_buffers play in PostgreSQL, per this lesson?
options: It sets how much memory PostgreSQL dedicates to caching table and index pages, the equivalent-purpose setting to SQL Server's buffer pool
It controls how many concurrent connections are allowed
It sets the maximum size of a single WAL segment
It configures replication lag tolerance
questions.explain: shared_buffers is PostgreSQL's shared memory cache for data pages, serving the same purpose as SQL Server's buffer pool.

questions.q: Why is the commonly cited shared_buffers starting point only around 25% of system RAM, rather than most of it?
options: PostgreSQL also relies heavily on the operating system's own filesystem cache for the rest
PostgreSQL cannot use more than 25% of RAM under any circumstance
Higher values always crash the server
25% is a hard-coded maximum enforced by PostgreSQL
questions.explain: Data not in shared_buffers often still comes from OS cache rather than actual disk I/O, so PostgreSQL doesn't need to claim most of the memory itself.

questions.q: Why is setting work_mem too high risky under heavy concurrent load, per this lesson?
options: work_mem applies per operation, and many concurrent queries can each claim their own allotment simultaneously, risking memory exhaustion
work_mem is a single global budget shared by the whole server, so it's always safe to raise
work_mem only affects VACUUM operations
work_mem has no effect on memory usage at all
questions.explain: Because work_mem is granted per sort/hash operation and a query can use multiple simultaneously, total memory use can multiply well beyond one query's apparent need.

options: It's a planner hint estimating total cacheable memory, and allocates no memory itself
It allocates dedicated memory for caching, separate from shared_buffers
It sets the maximum number of WAL segments retained
It controls autovacuum thresholds
questions.explain: effective_cache_size only informs the query planner's estimates about whether pages are likely already cached; it doesn't reserve any memory.

options: A separate, usually larger memory allowance for operations like VACUUM and CREATE INDEX
The memory budget for every SELECT query on the server
The amount of WAL PostgreSQL archives per segment
The size of the connection pool
questions.explain: PostgreSQL keeps a distinct budget for maintenance operations, which run less often than everyday queries but benefit from more memory when they do.
